prompt.context: A hospital group has been experiencing growing pains and has asked our firm for help.
prompt.question: The hospital group's profits are going down. Diagnose the root cause and recommend a course of action.

clarifying_info.q: What do you mean by growing pains?
clarifying_info.a: The hospital group originally consisted of one hospital and then it acquired 3 other hospitals, and its profits are going down.
Yes, the CEO of the main hospital changed; it was originally an MD doctor, now it is a business-experienced MBA.

clarifying_info.q: Any other changes or events impacting the hospital group?

exhibits.title: Survey of Doctors regarding hospital
exhibits.shows: Bar chart showing percentage of doctors holding Positive Opinion, No Opinion, or Negative Opinion about the hospital

exhibits.title: Issues Impacting Doctors
exhibits.shows: Bar chart showing percentage of doctors citing each issue as impacting them

framework: Scope: Determine whether profitability decline is in the main hospital or the acquired hospitals
Revenue vs. Cost: Isolate whether the issue is on the revenue side or cost side
Revenue deep-dive: Examine volume of patients, mix of services, and revenue per patient
Patient mix: Segment patients by insurance type (private, public, uninsured) and identify shifts
Referral drivers: Identify what drives private-insurance patients to the hospital (physician referrals)
Hypothesis: Link management change to physician perception change and lower referrals
Testing the hypothesis: Survey physicians to validate
Strategic response: Evaluate the hospital's billing outsourcing service as a tool to rebuild physician relationships
Economics: Perform cost-benefit analysis of billing outsourcing from the physician's perspective

questions.prompt: Step 1 – Where is the profitability decline occurring?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask whether the decline is in the main hospital or the acquired hospitals. Key insight: the acquired hospitals did not experience any profit decline, so the main hospital is the source of the problem.

questions.prompt: Step 2 – Is the main hospital's issue on the revenue side or the cost side?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose a profit = revenue – cost framework. The interviewer confirms costs have not changed, so revenue decline is the driver. Candidate should then focus exclusively on revenue.

questions.prompt: Step 3 – What is driving the revenue decline in the main hospital?
questions.guidance: Candidate should explore: (1) volume of patients – no change; (2) mix of services performed – no change; (3) revenue per patient – declining. This implies that patient mix in terms of payer type is shifting, with fewer private-insurance patients (who generate higher revenue) and more public-insurance or uninsured patients.

questions.prompt: Step 4 – What drives private-insurance patients to the hospital, and why might that have changed?
questions.guidance: Key driver of private-insurance patients is referrals from private physicians. Candidate should form the hypothesis: the change in CEO from an MD to an MBA may have altered physicians' perception of the hospital, leading to fewer referrals of private-insurance patients. Candidate should propose testing this via a physician survey.

questions.prompt: Step 5 – Interpret the physician survey results (Exhibits 1 and 2).
questions.guidance: Exhibit 1: The majority of surveyed doctors have no opinion (~65%) about the hospital, which is concerning because indifferent physicians are unlikely to actively refer patients. Only ~10% hold a positive opinion. Exhibit 2: The dominant issue plaguing doctors is billing complexity (~70%), which is an actionable opportunity for the hospital.

questions.prompt: Step 6 – The hospital has a billing outsourcing service it does not aggressively market to physicians. Evaluate whether this is a viable offering that could strengthen physician relationships.
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask for the economics of the physician's office before calculating. Strong candidates will ask for physician revenue (not just profit) and confirm whether additional costs are incurred when the physician frees up billing time.

math.setup: Physician annual revenue = $425,000; Profit = $175,000; Costs = $250,000. Time allocation: 75% patient care, 15% billing, 10% administrative. If billing is outsourced, the physician can redirect 15% of time to patient care. Since the physician currently earns $425,000 from 75% patient-care time, additional revenue = $425,000 × (15%/75%). Cost of outsourcing service = $50,000. No additional costs are incurred when adding the extra patient-care time.
steps: Net benefit to physician = $85,000 – $50,000 (cost of service) = $35,000
math.answer: ROI = 70%; New physician profit = $210,000; Profit increase = 20%

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key drivers that cause patients with private insurance to choose a particular hospital?

categories.name: Physician referrals
ideas: Relationships between hospital management and private physicians
Physician satisfaction with hospital administration and billing processes
Hospital reputation among the physician community

categories.name: Insurance network
ideas: Whether the hospital is in-network for major private insurers
Negotiated reimbursement rates attracting preferred providers

categories.name: Location and convenience
ideas: Proximity to affluent neighborhoods more likely to carry private insurance

recommendation: The main hospital is experiencing revenue decline due to a shift in patient mix toward lower-paying (public insurance or uninsured) patients, likely caused by fewer referrals from private physicians following the change in hospital management from an MD to an MBA.

To reverse the decline, the hospital should aggressively market its billing outsourcing service to private physicians, which delivers a 70% ROI within one year and increases physician profits by 20%, thereby rebuilding physician relationships and incentivizing more private-insurance referrals.
risks: Physician perception of management may require more than a single service offering to fully restore trust
Other hospitals may offer competing billing solutions or higher referral incentives
Implementation capacity: the hospital's billing outsourcing service must be able to scale to serve multiple physician practices
next_steps: Launch targeted outreach campaign to local private physicians presenting the billing outsourcing value proposition
Establish a physician liaison program under the new CEO to rebuild relationship capital
Track referral volumes by physician and insurance type monthly to measure impact
Evaluate whether similar relationship-building programs are needed for the acquired hospitals
